title: Real Analysis I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L Real Analysis I curriculum: the real number system and completeness, bounds/supremum/infimum, sequences and their limits, convergence tests, Cauchy sequences, infinite series, and continuity of real functions.

questions.question: Which property distinguishes the real numbers ℝ from the rational numbers ℚ?
options: ℝ is complete (every non-empty bounded-above subset has a least upper bound); ℚ is not
ℝ is countable while ℚ is not
ℚ is closed under addition while ℝ is not
questions.correct_answer: ℝ is complete (every non-empty bounded-above subset has a least upper bound); ℚ is not
questions.explanation: The Completeness (Least Upper Bound) Axiom is the defining property that separates ℝ from ℚ, e.g. √2 is a supremum in ℝ but has no rational supremum in ℚ.

questions.question: The supremum (least upper bound) of the set A = {x ∈ ℝ : x < 3} is:
questions.explanation: Although 3 is not in A, it is the smallest number that is an upper bound for every element of A, so sup(A) = 3.

questions.question: A set S ⊆ ℝ is bounded above if:
options: There exists M ∈ ℝ such that x ≤ M for all x ∈ S
There exists m ∈ ℝ such that x ≥ m for all x ∈ S
questions.correct_answer: There exists M ∈ ℝ such that x ≤ M for all x ∈ S
questions.explanation: Boundedness above means some real number M is at least as large as every element of S; such an M is called an upper bound.

questions.question: The infimum of the set S = {1/n : n ∈ ℕ, n ≥ 1} is:
questions.explanation: The values 1/n approach 0 as n increases without ever reaching it, and 0 is the greatest lower bound of the set.

questions.question: A sequence (an) is said to converge to a limit L if:
options: For every ε > 0, there exists N ∈ ℕ such that |an − L| < ε for all n > N
questions.correct_answer: For every ε > 0, there exists N ∈ ℕ such that |an − L| < ε for all n > N
questions.explanation: This is the formal epsilon-N definition of convergence: eventually, all terms lie within any prescribed distance ε of the limit L.

questions.question: What is lim(n→∞) 1/n?
questions.explanation: As n grows without bound, the terms 1/n shrink toward zero, so the sequence converges to 0.

questions.question: What is lim(n→∞) (n+1)/n?
questions.explanation: (n+1)/n = 1 + 1/n, and as n → ∞, 1/n → 0, so the whole expression approaches 1.

questions.question: Every convergent sequence of real numbers is necessarily:
questions.correct_answer: Bounded
questions.explanation: A standard theorem states convergence implies boundedness, though the converse is false (a bounded sequence need not converge).

questions.question: The Monotone Convergence Theorem states that:
options: Every bounded, monotonic sequence of real numbers converges
Every increasing sequence diverges to infinity
questions.correct_answer: Every bounded, monotonic sequence of real numbers converges
questions.explanation: A sequence that is both monotonic (increasing or decreasing) and bounded is guaranteed to converge, by completeness of ℝ.

questions.question: A sequence (an) is called a Cauchy sequence if:
options: For every ε > 0, there exists N such that |am − an| < ε for all m, n > N
questions.correct_answer: For every ε > 0, there exists N such that |am − an| < ε for all m, n > N
questions.explanation: A Cauchy sequence has terms that get arbitrarily close to each other (not just to a fixed limit) as the index grows.

questions.question: In ℝ, a sequence converges if and only if it is:
questions.correct_answer: A Cauchy sequence
questions.explanation: By the completeness of ℝ, a sequence of real numbers converges precisely when it is Cauchy; this is the Cauchy Criterion.

questions.question: The sequence an = (−1)^n is:
options: Bounded but divergent (it oscillates between −1 and 1)
questions.correct_answer: Bounded but divergent (it oscillates between −1 and 1)
questions.explanation: The sequence alternates between −1 and 1 forever without settling on a single limit, so it is bounded but does not converge.

questions.question: An infinite series Σan is said to converge if:
options: The sequence of partial sums Sn = a1 + a2 + ... + an converges to a finite limit
Every term an equals zero eventually
The series has finitely many nonzero terms
questions.correct_answer: The sequence of partial sums Sn = a1 + a2 + ... + an converges to a finite limit
questions.explanation: Convergence of a series is defined via the limit of its sequence of partial sums.

questions.question: The geometric series Σ r^n (n = 0 to ∞) converges if and only if:
questions.explanation: A geometric series converges exactly when the common ratio has absolute value less than 1, in which case it sums to 1/(1−r).

questions.question: The sum of the geometric series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... is:
questions.explanation: This is a geometric series with a = 1 and r = 1/2, so the sum is a/(1−r) = 1/(1− 0.5) = 2.

questions.question: The harmonic series Σ 1/n (n = 1 to ∞):
options: Diverges, even though its terms tend to 0
questions.correct_answer: Diverges, even though its terms tend to 0
questions.explanation: A classical result: although 1/n → 0, the harmonic series' partial sums grow without bound, so the series diverges.

questions.question: According to the nth-term (divergence) test, if lim(n→∞) an ≠ 0, then the series Σan:
questions.correct_answer: Must diverge
questions.explanation: If the terms of a series do not tend to zero, the series cannot converge; this is a necessary (not sufficient) condition for convergence.

questions.question: The p-series Σ 1/n^p (n = 1 to ∞) converges if and only if:
questions.explanation: The p-series test states convergence occurs precisely when the exponent p exceeds 1; p = 1 gives the divergent harmonic series.

questions.question: A series Σan is called absolutely convergent if:
questions.correct_answer: Σ|an| converges
questions.explanation: Absolute convergence requires the series of absolute values to converge, which is a stronger condition than ordinary convergence.

questions.question: A function f is continuous at a point c if:
options: f is defined only at c
questions.correct_answer: lim(x→c) f(x) = f(c)
questions.explanation: Continuity at a point requires that the limit as x approaches c exists and equals the function's actual value there.

questions.question: Using the epsilon-delta definition, f is continuous at c if for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that:
options: δ depends only on f(c), not on ε
questions.correct_answer: |x − c| < δ implies |f(x) − f(c)| < ε
questions.explanation: This is the precise epsilon-delta formulation: x sufficiently close to c (within δ) forces f(x) to be within ε of f(c).

questions.question: The function f(x) = 1/x is discontinuous at x = 0 because:
options: f is not defined at x = 0
f(0) = 0 but the limit is different
f is continuous everywhere including x = 0
questions.correct_answer: f is not defined at x = 0
questions.explanation: Since 1/x has no value at x = 0 (division by zero is undefined), continuity there fails trivially, and the limit also does not exist as a finite number.

questions.question: The Intermediate Value Theorem states that if f is continuous on [a, b] and k is any value between f(a) and f(b), then:
options: There exists c ∈ [a, b] such that f(c) = k
questions.correct_answer: There exists c ∈ [a, b] such that f(c) = k
questions.explanation: The IVT guarantees a continuous function on a closed interval attains every value between its endpoint values.

questions.question: The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that a continuous function on a closed, bounded interval [a, b]:
options: Attains both a maximum and a minimum value on [a, b]
questions.correct_answer: Attains both a maximum and a minimum value on [a, b]
questions.explanation: Continuity on a compact (closed and bounded) interval ensures the function achieves both its supremum and infimum as actual values.

questions.question: A set S ⊆ ℝ is called dense in ℝ if:
options: Every open interval of ℝ contains an element of S
questions.correct_answer: Every open interval of ℝ contains an element of S
questions.explanation: Density means elements of S can be found arbitrarily close to any real number; the rationals ℚ are a classic dense subset of ℝ.

questions.question: The Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem states that:
options: Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence
Every unbounded sequence has a limit
questions.correct_answer: Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence
questions.explanation: This foundational compactness result guarantees a convergent subsequence exists whenever the original sequence is bounded.

questions.question: If lim(n→∞) an = L and lim(n→∞) bn = M, then lim(n→∞) (an + bn) equals:
questions.correct_answer: L + M
questions.explanation: By the algebra-of-limits theorem, the limit of a sum of convergent sequences equals the sum of their individual limits.

questions.question: The set of natural numbers ℕ is:
options: Unbounded above in ℝ, by the Archimedean Property
questions.correct_answer: Unbounded above in ℝ, by the Archimedean Property
questions.explanation: The Archimedean Property states that for any real number x, there exists a natural number n greater than x, so ℕ has no upper bound in ℝ.

questions.question: Alternating series test: the series Σ(−1)^n / n converges because:
options: Its terms decrease in absolute value to 0 while alternating in sign
questions.correct_answer: Its terms decrease in absolute value to 0 while alternating in sign
questions.explanation: The Alternating Series Test guarantees convergence when terms alternate in sign, decrease in magnitude, and tend to zero — conditions satisfied by 1/n; note this series is only conditionally, not absolutely, convergent.

questions.question: If f and g are both continuous at x = c, then which of the following is also necessarily continuous at c?
options: None of these combinations are continuous
questions.correct_answer: f + g
questions.explanation: Sums of continuous functions are always continuous; quotients require the denominator to be nonzero at the point in question.
